examples.english: He is there. / He is not there.

examples.irish: Chonaic mé é. / Ní fhaca mé é.
examples.english: I saw it. / I didn't see it.

examples.irish: Rinne sí é. / Ní dhearna sí é.
examples.english: She did it. / She didn't do it.

examples.irish: Fuair mé é. / Ní bhfuair mé é.
examples.english: I got it. / I didn't get it.

examples.irish: Tá a fhios agam go bhfuil sé fíor.
examples.english: I know that it is true. (go + dep. form)
I see that you don't understand.
Did you eat your dinner? (ar + past dep.)

notes: The dependent/independent distinction is pervasive — it affects every sentence with a negative, question, or subordinating particle. The most important pairs to master: tá/bhfuil, bhí/raibh, beidh/mbeidh, chonaic/bhfaca, chuaigh/ndeachaigh, rinne/ndearna, fuair/bhfuair, tháinig/dtáinig. These irregular dependent stems must be memorised.

title: The Relative Future & Autonomous Relative
summary: In relative clauses with future or habitual meaning, Irish uses special relative forms — 'a dhéanfas', 'a bheidh', 'a ólas'. These differ from the ordinary future tense forms.
content:
When a future or habitual verb appears in a relative clause, Irish traditionally uses a special RELATIVE form, distinct from the ordinary future tense.

Ordinary future: ólfaidh sé     he will drink
Relative future: an fear a ólas  the man who will drink

Relative future formation — 1st conjugation:
  broad:   -as    ólann → a ólas   (who drinks/will drink)
  slender: -eas   itheann → a itheas  (who eats)

Relative future formation — 2nd conjugation:
  ceannaigh → a cheannós
  éirigh → a éireós

Irregular relative futures:
  bí:    a bheidh  (who will be) — same as ordinary future
  déan:  a dhéanfas  (who will do)
  téigh: a rachfas  (who will go)
  tar:   a thiocfas  (who will come)
  abair: a déarfas  (who will say)
  faigh: a gheobhas  (who will get)
  feic:  a fheicfeas (who will see)

The relative future is used:
1. In subject/object relative clauses with future meaning:
   an duine a thiocfas    the person who will come
   an rud a dhéanfas tú  the thing you will do
   an lá a bheidh muid ann  the day we will be there

2. In proverbs and general truths (habitual relative):
   An té a bheidh thuas, óltar deoch air; an té a bheidh thíos, buailfear cic air.
   He who is up gets a drink; he who is down gets a kick.

3. After certain conjunctions with future/habitual reference:
   nuair a thiocfas sé    when he comes
   sula n-imeochaidh sé   before he goes
   más maith leat         if you like (relative of 'is')

Note: In modern spoken Irish, the ordinary future form is frequently used in place of the relative future, especially outside formal/literary contexts. The relative future sounds more formal and is more common in writing, prayers, proverbs, and Munster Irish.

examples.irish: An fear a thiocfas ar dtús.
examples.english: The man who will come first.

examples.irish: An rud a dhéanfas tú amárach.
examples.english: The thing you will do tomorrow.
The one who will be there.

examples.irish: An duine a ólas an iomarca.
examples.english: The person who drinks too much.

examples.irish: An lá a rachfas muid go hÉirinn.
examples.english: The day we will go to Ireland.

examples.irish: An té a léas é, tuigfidh sé.

notes: The relative future is one of the markers that distinguishes formal/literary Irish from everyday speech. It is very common in Munster Irish and in traditional texts, prayers, and proverbs. Learners at C1 should be able to recognise and produce it, even if they default to the ordinary future in casual speech.

title: Word Formation: Prefixes & Suffixes
summary: Irish has a rich system of prefixes and suffixes for forming new words. Knowing these allows you to expand vocabulary systematically and understand unfamiliar words.
content:
PREFIXES — added to the beginning of a word:

Negating / reversing:
  mí-    bad, mis-, un-    míshásta (unhappy), míchuí (inappropriate)
  neamh- non-, un-        neamhspleách (independent), neamhfhoirmiúil (informal)
  an-    very, intensive  an-mhaith (very good), an-mhór (very big)
         [note: an- triggers lenition]
  ró-    too, over-       rómhall (too slow), rómhór (too big)

Repetition / back:
  ath-   re-, again       athléamh (re-reading), athnuachan (renewal)

Former / past:
  iar-   former, ex-      iar-uachtarán (former president), iarchéimí (postgraduate)
  sean-  old, former      seanfhocal (proverb, lit. old word), seanduine (old person)

Half / co-:
  leath- half             leathuair (half hour), leathchéad (fifty, lit. half hundred)
  comh-  co-, jointly     comhairle (advice/council), comhoibriú (cooperation)

SUFFIXES — added to the end of a word:

Nouns from adjectives / verbal roots:
  -acht  (f.) abstract noun   saoire → saorántacht (citizenship)
                              Gaeilge → Gaeilgeacht (Irish-speaking area/culture)
                              flaithiúil → flaithiúlacht (generosity)
  -as    (m.) abstract noun   líonmhar → líonmharas (abundance)

Agent nouns (person who does X):
  -óir/-eoir  dochtúir? No — óir is the suffix:
              múin → múinteoir (teacher)
              ól → óltóir (drinker)
              léigh → léitheoir (reader)
              scríobh → scríbhneoir (writer)
  -aí/-í      ceolaí (musician), ealaíontóir (artist, from ealaín)

Diminutives (small / affectionate):
  -ín   cailín (girl, from caile), leabhrán? — mostly lexicalised
        bádín (little boat), Máirín (little Máire — a name)
        Pádraigín (nickname/diminutive of Pádraig)
  -án   gasúrán (little boy), ciotán (left-hander, from ciotach)

Place / abstract:
  -lann  place for an activity  leabharlann (library), pictiúrlann (cinema)
                                ospidéal ← Latin; but bialann (restaurant, from bia+lann)
  -ach   person from / relating to  Éireannach (Irish person), Francach (French person)

Verb-forming suffix:
  -aigh/-igh  form verbs from nouns/adjectives:
              glan (clean, adj.) → glanaigh (to clean)
              nua (new) → nuaigh? — not all work

examples.irish: Tá sé míshásta leis an gcinneadh.
examples.english: He is unhappy with the decision. (mí- prefix)
It is too difficult. (ró- prefix + lenition)
It is very good altogether. (an- prefix + lenition)

notes: The suffix -acht is extremely productive for abstract nouns and is worth learning as a pattern: any adjective can potentially take -acht to form an abstract noun. The -óir/-eoir suffix is the main agent noun suffix. The prefix an- (very) is ubiquitous in speech but triggers lenition — 'an-mhaith', not 'an-maith'.

title: Genitive Chains & Complex Noun Phrases
summary: Irish builds complex noun phrases by chaining genitives. Only the final noun in the chain takes the definite article; the intermediate nouns are in genitive without an article.
content:
In a genitive chain, one noun modifies another in the genitive case. The rules:

1. Only the LAST element in a chain can take the definite article
2. Intermediate nouns appear in the genitive without an article
3. The first noun is in the nominative; each subsequent noun is in the genitive of the preceding one

Simple two-noun genitive:
  teach an fhir     the man's house
  (nominative: teach; genitive: an fhir)

Three-noun chain:
  teach mháthair an fhir     the house of the man's mother
  (teach = nom; mháthair = gen of máthair; an fhir = gen of fear)
  Note: máthair has no article — only the final noun gets it

Four-noun chain (formal/written):
  ceannaire an choiste stiúrtha    chairman of the steering committee
  (ceannaire = nom; an choiste = gen; stiúrtha = gen of stiúrú)

Key rules:
  - Masculine genitive singular: usually slenderise final consonant
    fear → fir;  bord → boird;  Rí → Rí (vowel-final, no change)
  - Feminine genitive singular: lenition, often -e suffix
    bean → mná (irreg.);  súil → súla;  léim → léime
  - Definite genitive: an + lenition (masc.) / na + h- before vowel (fem.)
    an fhir (the man's);  na mná (the woman's);  na hoíche (of the night)
  - Indefinite genitive: no article, same lenition/slenderisation
    teach fir (a man's house)
  - Verbal noun genitive objects:
    ag léamh leabhair    reading a book  (leabhair = gen of leabhar)
    ag ól uisce          drinking water  (uisce = gen of uisce; vowel, no change)
    ag déanamh oibre     doing work      (oibre = gen of obair)

Compound nouns — the modifying noun goes in genitive:
  clár ama         timetable    (clár + gen. of am)
  lá breithe       birthday     (lá + gen. of breith)
  rang Gaeilge     Irish class  (rang + gen. of Gaeilge)
  teach ósta       hotel        (teach + gen. of ósta)
  baile mór        town         (lit. big town — adjective, not genitive)
  ceol tíre        country music (ceol + gen. of tír)
  cúrsaí oideachais  educational matters  (cúrsaí + gen. of oideachas)

examples.english: Reading a book. (verbal noun + genitive object)
The door of the big house.

notes: The 'only the last noun gets the article' rule catches learners constantly — 'an teach an fhir' is wrong; it must be 'teach an fhir'. Similarly with verbal nouns: 'ag léamh an leabhair' (reading the book — definite) vs. 'ag léamh leabhair' (reading a book — indefinite genitive). Genitive chains are ubiquitous in formal and written Irish.

title: Complex Conjunctions: Concessive, Causal & Temporal
summary: Beyond the basic conjunctions (agus, ach, mar), Irish has a rich set of complex conjunctions for expressing concession, cause, condition, and time. These are essential for expressing nuanced ideas.
content:
CONCESSIVE — 'although / even though / despite'

  cé go + eclipsis     although (+ present/future)
  cé gur + lenition    although (+ past)
  cé go raibh          although (+ past bí)
  in ainneoin go       despite the fact that
  d'ainneoin go        despite / notwithstanding
  fiú agus             even though
  ach oiread           no more than, not even

  Cé go bhfuil sé deacair, is fiú é.    Although it is difficult, it is worth it.
  D'ainneoin go raibh sé tuirseach, lean sé air.
    Despite being tired, he continued.

CAUSAL — 'because / since / given that'

  mar     because (most common, informal)
  toisc   because, owing to (+ go/gur)
  ó       since, because (often used for logical reason)
  ó tharla (go)  since it happened that / given that
  de bharr go    because of, due to
  de bhrí go     because, for the reason that (formal)
  os rud é go    seeing as, given that (formal)

  Ní raibh sé ann mar bhí sé tinn.    He wasn't there because he was sick.
  Ó tharla go raibh sé ann, labhair mé leis.   Since he was there, I spoke to him.
  Os rud é go bhfuil sé déanta, lean ar aghaidh.   Since it is done, continue.

TEMPORASL — 'when / while / until / before / after / as soon as'

  nuair a + dep.         when (specific event)
  fad is / fad a         while, as long as
  go dtí go              until (+ eclipsis)
  sula / sara + eclipsis before
  tar éis do X + VN      after X does/did
  chomh luath agus       as soon as
  i ndiaidh do X + VN    after X does/did
  ón uair go             since (temporal: from the time that)

  Nuair a thiocfaidh sé, abair leis fanacht.
    When he comes, tell him to wait.
  Fan go dtí go dtagann sé.    Wait until he comes.
  Chomh luath agus a tháinig sé, d'imigh sí.
    As soon as he arrived, she left.
  Tar éis dó imeacht, bhí ciúnas ann.
    After he left, there was silence.

COMPARATIVE / PROPORTIONAL:
  dá + comparative…, is + comparative…
  Dá mhéad airgid atá agat, is mó a chaithfidh tú.
  The more money you have, the more you will spend.

examples.english: He wasn't there because he was sick.

Os rud é go bhfuil sé ráite, ná habair a thuilleadh.

Fad is a bheidh mé beo.

notes: The 'tar éis do X + verbal noun' construction is very important — it is one of the main ways to express 'after doing something'. The dá...is (the more...the more) construction is a calque of a pan-Celtic pattern. Os rud é go and ó tharla go are formal register markers that signal a careful, educated speaker.

title: An tOileánach — Tomás Ó Criomhthain
summary: The autobiography of a Blasket Islander, written in Munster Irish. One of the foundational texts of modern Irish literature. First published 1929.
content:
Tomás Ó Criomhthain (1856–1937) was a native speaker from the Great Blasket Island off the Kerry coast. At the urging of scholars who recognised that his way of life — and language — was vanishing, he wrote his autobiography. The result is a masterpiece of unselfconscious prose: vivid, laconic, and deeply rooted in the rhythms of island life.

Language: Classic Munster Irish (Corca Dhuibhne/Kerry dialect). Rich in idiomatic expression, with archaic forms not found in modern spoken Irish. Heavy use of synthetic verb forms. The vocabulary of fishing, farming, weather, and community.

Why read it: Ó Criomhthain's style is direct and unadorned — he never writes a word more than is needed. The prose has the quality of speech transcribed by a master. For learners, it is a window into both the language and the world it described.

The final line of the book is among the most quoted in Irish literature:
  'Ní bheidh ár leithéidí arís ann.'
  (Our like will not be there again.)

Where to read: Available from Clóchomhar (Irish) and Oxford University Press (English translation by Robin Flower, 'The Islandman'). The Irish text is in print and widely available.

examples.irish: Ní bheidh ár leithéidí arís ann.
examples.english: Our like will not be there again.
examples.note: The famous closing line

examples.irish: Ní raibh aon bhád ag imeacht an lá sin agus ní raibh súil agam le haon bhád.
examples.english: There was no boat going that day and I had no expectation of any boat.

examples.irish: Is iomaí lá a bhíos ag féachaint ar an bhfarraige agus í ag gluaiseacht is ag borradh.
examples.english: Many a day I would be watching the sea as it moved and swelled.
examples.note: Note the synthetic past habitual 'bhíos' (I used to be) — Munster 1sg form

examples.irish: Bíodh sin mar atá, ní hé an duine sona an duine a bhíonn gan bhuaireamh.
examples.english: Be that as it may, the happy person is not the one who is without trouble.

notes: Best approached after solid B2/C1 Munster Irish. The synthetic verb forms (bhíos, chonacs, chualamar) will be unfamiliar to learners of Standard Irish but become readable quickly. Robin Flower's English translation is beautiful in its own right and useful as a crib. Séamas Ó Duilearga's scholarly edition has glosses.

title: Peig — Peig Sayers
summary: The autobiography of storyteller Peig Sayers, dictated in Kerry Irish and transcribed by her son. Rich in oral formulaic expression and seanfhocail. First published 1936.
content:
Peig Sayers (1873–1958) was one of the greatest traditional storytellers (seanchaí) of the twentieth century, also from the Great Blasket Island. Unlike Ó Criomhthain, she did not write — her autobiography was dictated to her son Micheál and transcribed. This gives the prose a different quality: the rhythms of oral storytelling, with its formulaic phrases, rhetorical questions, and direct address to the listener.

For decades, Peig was compulsory on the Irish Leaving Certificate syllabus. This association — and the unrelenting bleakness of much of the narrative — made it notorious. In fact, read without the pressure of exams, it is a remarkable document of an oral tradition that had survived continuously from medieval Ireland.

Language: Rich Munster Irish (Kerry). Extremely idiomatic. Full of seanfhocail (proverbs), which Peig deployed constantly in conversation. More syntactically complex than Ó Criomhthain — longer sentences, more subordinate clauses.

Where to read: In print from An Sagart. English translation by Bryan MacMahon ('Peig: The Autobiography of Peig Sayers of the Great Blasket Island').

examples.irish: Ní bhíonn an rath ach mar a mbíonn an smacht.
examples.english: Prosperity is only where there is discipline. (proverb she quotes)

examples.irish: Is minic a bhí mé ag machnamh ar an saol is ar an mbás.
examples.english: Many a time I was thinking about life and death.

examples.irish: Ó! a dhuine chóir, is í an tsláinte an rud is fearr ar domhan.
examples.english: Oh! good person, health is the best thing in the world.
examples.note: Vocative 'a dhuine chóir' — direct address typical of oral style

examples.irish: Tá sé ráite go minic: 'Is glas iad na cnoic i bhfad uainn.'
examples.english: It is often said: 'Far-away hills are green.'
examples.note: Classic seanfhocal — proverb

notes: The oral formulaic style is the key feature. Peig addresses the reader directly ('a dhuine chóir'), uses proverbs as punctuation, and structures narratives around traditional storytelling patterns. For learners of seanfhocail and rhetorical Irish, it is unparalleled. The notoriety as a school text is a distraction — approach it on its own terms.

title: Fiche Blian ag Fás — Muiris Ó Súilleabháin
summary: A lyrical memoir of growing up on the Great Blasket Island, written in vivid, youthful prose. Often considered the most accessible and joyful of the Blasket texts. First published 1933.
content:
Muiris Ó Súilleabháin (1904–1950) wrote 'Fiche Blian ag Fás' (Twenty Years A-Growing) while still a young man, at the encouragement of George Thomson, a Cambridge classicist who had spent time on the island. The book was simultaneously published in Irish and in English translation by Moya Llewelyn Davies and George Thomson, with a preface by E.M. Forster.

Unlike the older Blasket autobiographers, Muiris writes with the exuberance of youth. The prose is lyrical, sometimes poetic, rich in sensory detail, and lit by his obvious delight in language and story.

Language: Munster Irish (Kerry). Syntactically somewhat more accessible than Ó Criomhthain's more lapidary style, though equally idiomatic. Good use of direct speech.

Forster's preface called it 'an account of neolithic civilisation from the inside'. Whatever one thinks of that framing, the book captures a vanished world with extraordinary freshness.

Where to read: In print from Clóchomhar (Irish). English translation widely available.

examples.irish: Bhí an lá breá, an ghrian ag taitneamh go glé ar an uisce.
examples.english: The day was fine, the sun shining brightly on the water.

examples.irish: Tháinig áthas orm nár airigh mé a leithéid riamh roimhe.
examples.english: A joy came upon me the like of which I had never felt before.

examples.irish: Ní raibh sé de nós againn morán cainte a dhéanamh ar an ábhar sin.
examples.english: It was not our custom to say much on that subject.

examples.irish: Is é mo thuairim go raibh gach uile dhuine ar an oileán sona sásta.
examples.english: It is my opinion that every single person on the island was happy and content.

notes: The most accessible starting point of the three Blasket autobiographies — the youthful voice makes it easier to stay with. E.M. Forster's English-language preface is worth reading for context. Muiris later emigrated to the Irish mainland and drowned in 1950. The book stands as a document of a world that effectively ended when the island was evacuated in 1953.

title: Cré na Cille — Máirtín Ó Cadhain
summary: A modernist novel set entirely among the dead in a Connemara graveyard. Considered the greatest prose work in Irish. Demands fluency and comfort with Connemara dialect. First published 1949.
content:
Máirtín Ó Cadhain (1906–1970) was a native speaker from Connemara who became a professor of Irish at Trinity College Dublin. 'Cré na Cille' (Graveyard Clay / The Dirty Dust) is the undisputed masterpiece of Irish-language fiction.

The entire novel takes place underground in a Connemara graveyard, where the dead gossip, quarrel, and obsess over the world above. There is no narrator — only voices. The technique is close to what Beckett was doing at exactly the same time, and the two writers were aware of each other.

Language: Connemara Irish — the Cois Fharraige dialect — at its most dense and idiomatic. Enormous vocabulary, rapid register shifts, satire, poetry, and profanity all mixed together. It is not a book for learners who are not already fluent; it is a book for those who want to understand what Irish can do.

Bruno Mac Con Iomaire and Tim Robinson's English translation ('The Dirty Dust', 2015) finally made it accessible to non-Irish readers and is worth reading alongside the original.

Where to read: In print from An Clóchomhar. English translation from Yale University Press.

examples.irish: Murar tháinig sé anseo fós, tiocfaidh sé.
examples.english: If he hasn't come here yet, he will come.
examples.note: A voice from the grave, waiting for a new arrival

examples.irish: Ach an tsíocháin! An tsíocháin! Tá sí chomh gann anseo agus a bhí sí thuas.
examples.english: But peace! Peace! It is as scarce here as it was above.

examples.irish: Cén mhaith dom labhairt? Ní éisteann aon duine liom.
examples.english: What good is it for me to speak? No one listens to me.

examples.irish: Ní raibh mé chomh sona riamh — ach anois, b'fhéidir.
examples.english: I was never so happy — but now, perhaps.

notes: Do not attempt without C1+ Irish. The voices are dense, overlapping, and assume knowledge of Connemara social structures. The reward is extraordinary — Ó Cadhain's range of register, from high rhetoric to bitter comedy, has no equal in modern Irish. The English translation by Mac Con Iomaire and Robinson is the best English prose written from an Irish-language source.

title: Cúirt an Mheán Oíche — Brian Merriman
summary: An 18th-century comic-satirical poem in which the women of Ireland put men on trial for failing to marry them. Ribald, brilliant, and one of the longest poems in Irish. Written c. 1780.
content:
Brian Merriman (c. 1747–1805) was a Clare schoolmaster who wrote this 1,026-line poem — the longest poem in Irish — around 1780. It was not published in print until 1904, having circulated in manuscript. It uses the aisling (vision poem) form, in which the poet falls asleep and is visited by a supernatural figure — here, Aoibheall, queen of the Munster fairies, who presides over a court of women prosecuting Irish men.

The poem is comic, satirical, sexually frank, and formally accomplished. It mocks clerical celibacy, male laziness, and the institution of marriage with equal relish.

Language: East Clare Irish of the late 18th century — close to modern Munster Irish but with archaic forms and a heightened, bardic register. The verse form is syllabic with internal rhyme, quite different from English stress-metre.

Where to read: The standard edition is Dáithí Ó hÓgáin's. Frank O'Connor's English translation ('The Midnight Court') is famous and free-spirited. Ciaran Carson's translation is more recent and more literal.

Famous opening lines:
  Ba gnáth mé ag siúl le ciumhais na habhann
  Ar bháinseach úr is an drúcht go trom…

examples.irish: Ba gnáth mé ag siúl le ciumhais na habhann / Ar bháinseach úr is an drúcht go trom.
examples.english: I used to walk along the river's edge / On fresh meadow with the dew heavy.
examples.note: Opening lines — the standard aisling setting

examples.irish: Is fada liom féin mar tháinig an scéal / Go hóg gan chéile mé ag méadú i ngéibheann.
examples.english: Long it seems to me how the tale has come / That I am young without a spouse, growing in distress.

examples.irish: Táimid i bpian is i bpurgadóir / Ag fanacht le fear nach bhfuil i bhfonn orainn.
examples.english: We are in pain and in purgatory / Waiting for a man who has no inclination towards us.
examples.note: The women's complaint

notes: The sexual frankness of the poem shocked 19th-century editors — the first printed edition omitted 'offensive' passages. Read whole or not at all. The Frank O'Connor English version takes liberties but captures the spirit. For learners of literary Munster Irish, the verse form is worth studying: the couplets rhyme on stressed vowels, not word-endings.

title: Nuala Ní Dhomhnaill — Selected Poems
summary: The foremost contemporary Irish-language poet. Her work draws on mythology, feminism, and the unconscious in rich, accessible Munster Irish. Essential for anyone serious about Irish literature.
content:
Nuala Ní Dhomhnaill (born 1952) grew up partly in the Kerry Gaeltacht and is the most widely translated Irish-language poet alive. Her work is grounded in the Munster oral tradition but reaches toward surrealism, feminist mythology, and the erotic in ways that are entirely contemporary.

She has been particularly important for making Irish-language poetry visible internationally through facing-page translations — by Seamus Heaney, Paul Muldoon, Ciaran Carson, and others — in volumes like 'The Astrakhan Cloak' and 'The Water Horse'.

Key collections:
  Féar Suaithinseach (1984)
  Feis (1991)
  Cead Aighnis (1998)
  The Fifty Minute Mermaid (2007)

Language: Contemporary Munster Irish with strong oral roots. More accessible than the Blasket writers — the syntax is modern, the vocabulary alive. An excellent place to develop a feeling for the music of Munster Irish.

Signature poems: 'An Mhaighdean Mhara' (The Mermaid), 'Ceist na Teangan' (The Language Issue), 'Féar Suaithinseach' (Miraculous Grass), 'Mo Mháthair' (My Mother).

examples.irish: Cuirim mo dhóchas ar snámh / i mbáidín teangan / faoi mar a leagfá naíonán / i gcliabhán.
examples.english: I place my hope on the water / in a little boat / of the language, / the way a body might put / an infant
examples.note: Opening of 'Ceist na Teangan' (The Language Issue) — her most anthologised poem

examples.irish: Is tú mo chuid den tsaol, a chuid / a chumann is a stór.
examples.english: You are my portion of the world, my share / my darling and my treasure.

examples.irish: Tá tú ag teacht isteach orm mar a thagann an fharraige / isteach ar thrá.
examples.english: You are coming in on me like the sea / comes in on a strand.

notes: The facing-page translation volumes are the ideal way in — read the Irish, look at the English, go back to the Irish. Seamus Heaney's translations in 'The Astrakhan Cloak' are particularly fine. 'Ceist na Teangan' (The Language Issue) is the essential starting poem — it addresses the precariousness of the Irish language directly and memorably.

title: Seán Ó Ríordáin — Selected Poems
summary: The most important Irish-language modernist poet. Dense, philosophical, and rooted in an anguished Munster Irish. Demands close reading and comfort with complex syntax.
content:
Seán Ó Ríordáin (1916–1977) was a Cork native who spent much of his adult life ill with tuberculosis. Out of that isolation he produced three collections of poetry that transformed what Irish-language poetry could do — bringing existentialism, self-consciousness about language, and a radical interiority that had no precedent in the tradition.

His diary (published posthumously) is also essential reading — in it he works out his ideas about language, identity, and the relationship between Irish and English in a voice of extraordinary honesty.

Key collections:
  Eireaball Spideoige (1952) — Robin's Tail
  Brosna (1964)
  Línte Liombó (1971)

Language: Dense, syntactically complex Munster Irish. He coinages new words, bends syntax to his needs, and refuses the expected. Not an entry-level text — but rewards the effort immensely.

Signature poems: 'Adhlacadh Mo Mháthar' (My Mother's Burial), 'Saoirse' (Freedom), 'Fill Arís' (Return Again), 'Claíomh Solais' (Sword of Light), 'Oíche Nollag' (Christmas Night).

examples.irish: Táim i gcathair idirdhealaithe, / I gcathair na n-athfhriotal.
examples.english: I am in a city of distinctions, / In a city of echoes.
examples.note: From 'Fill Arís' — on the position of the Irish speaker

examples.irish: Ná clois le glór na Gaeilge, / Ach éist le ciúnas na Gaeilge.
examples.english: Don't listen to the sound of Irish, / But listen to the silence of Irish.
examples.note: On the deeper reality of the language — one of his most quoted lines

examples.irish: Is fearr liom bheith im' dheoraí / ná fanacht mar seo im' cheartlár.
examples.english: I prefer to be an exile / than to remain like this at my centre.

notes: Approach after Ní Dhomhnaill — she is more accessible. Ó Ríordáin rewards slow, repeated reading. The bilingual edition with translations by Greg Delanty and Seán Ó Coileáin is the best introduction. His famous image of the poet as 'cat i measc madraí' (a cat among dogs) — the Irish speaker in an English world — runs through all his work.

title: An Giall — Brendan Behan
summary: Brendan Behan's play about an English soldier held hostage by the IRA, written first in Irish. The Irish original is sharper and more political than the later English adaptation 'The Hostage'.
content:
Brendan Behan (1923–1964) wrote 'An Giall' in Irish in 1957, at the request of Gael Linn and the director Tomás Mac Anna for the Damer Theatre in Dublin. The following year he adapted and expanded it as 'The Hostage' for Joan Littlewood's Theatre Workshop in London — transforming a taut political drama into a more expansive, music-hall influenced piece.

The Irish original is in many ways a stronger play: tighter, more politically serious, more genuinely bilingual in its treatment of language as subject matter. An English soldier held in a Dublin boarding house while an IRA man awaits execution — the Irish and English languages themselves become part of the drama.

Behan was a native Dublin Irish speaker (he had learned it in Borstal from Kerry prisoners) and the play's Irish has a distinctive Dublin flavour — colloquial, urban, marked by English loanwords and syntax, quite unlike the Gaeltacht varieties.

Language: Dublin Hiberno-Irish. Colloquial, full of English loanwords, fast-moving dialogue. A useful corrective to an over-literary view of what Irish is — this is the language of a city man who learned it unconventionally.

Where to read/see: Published by Chomhairle na Gaeilge. The An Giall / The Hostage volume from Gallery Press includes both versions.

examples.irish: Is Sasanach mise, ach ní naimhde muid go léir.
examples.english: I am English, but we are not all enemies.
examples.note: The hostage speaking — the central tension of the play

examples.irish: Tá an Ghaeilge chomh maith le haon teanga eile ar domhan.
examples.english: Irish is as good as any other language in the world.

examples.irish: Cén fáth nach bhféadfaimis a bheith ina gcairde?

notes: The comparison between 'An Giall' and 'The Hostage' is itself a literary study in what translation does to a work. Behan's Irish was unconventional — he had absorbed it from Kerry speakers and it has a different music from either Munster or Connacht literary Irish. For learners who want a non-Gaeltacht model of literary Irish, this is valuable.

title: Yes and No: Echoing the Verb
summary: Irish has no single word for 'yes' or 'no' — you answer by repeating the verb.
content:
Irish does not have dedicated words for 'yes' or 'no'. Instead, you answer a question by repeating the main verb (affirmative or negative). The verb form used must match the tense and person of the question.

PRESENT (bí):
  An bhfuil tú go maith?  →  Tá. / Níl.
  Are you well?          →  Yes. / No.

PAST:
  An raibh tú ann?  →  Bhí. / Ní raibh.
  Were you there?   →  Yes. / No.

FUTURE:
  An mbeidh tú ann?  →  Beidh. / Ní bheidh.
  Will you be there?  →  Yes. / No.

REGULAR VERBS:
  An gceannóidh tú é?  →  Ceannóidh. / Ní cheannóidh.
  An ndearna tú é?     →  Rinne. / Ní dhearna.

COPULA (is):
  An múinteoir thú?  →  Is ea. / Ní hea.
  Are you a teacher?  →  Yes (I am). / No (I'm not).

The answer verb must agree in tense with the question verb — you cannot answer a past-tense question with a present-tense verb.

examples.irish: An raibh tú sa bhaile? — Bhí.
An dtéann tú ar scoil? — Téim.
examples.english: Do you go to school? — Yes (I go).

examples.irish: An ndéanfaidh tú é? — Déanfaidh. / Ní dhéanfaidh.
examples.english: Will you do it? — Yes / No.
Is she a teacher? — Yes (she is).

notes: For copula questions, Is ea / Ní hea are the standard answers regardless of person. For all other verbs, the answer verb must be 3sg if the question was 3sg, etc. — though in practice speakers often use a fixed person.

title: Conjunctions (Cónascairí)
summary: Conjunctions link clauses and phrases. Many Irish conjunctions trigger mutations on the following verb.
content:
COORDINATING CONJUNCTIONS (linking equal clauses):
  agus  — and (no mutation)
  ach   — but (no mutation)
  nó    — or (no mutation)
  óir   — for, because (formal; no mutation)

SUBORDINATING CONJUNCTIONS (introducing dependent clauses):
  nuair  — when        → lenition of following verb: nuair a tháinig sé
  mar    — because, as → lenition: mar a dúirt mé
  sula   — before      → eclipsis: sula mbeidh sé déanach
  mura   — if not, unless → eclipsis: mura dtiocfaidh sé
  cé go  — although   → eclipsis: cé go bhfuil sé fuar
  ionas go — so that  → eclipsis: ionas go mbeidh sé réidh
  go dtí go — until   → eclipsis: go dtí go dtiocfaidh tú

CONDITIONAL:
  má    — if (real condition) → lenition: má tá tú sásta
  dá    — if (hypothetical)  → eclipsis/lenition depending on tense: dá mbeadh sé ann

The particle 'a' often appears between the conjunction and the verb for nuair/mar:
  nuair a + lenition (most common written form)
  nuair is also written as 'nuair a' before verbal forms.

examples.irish: Tá mé tuirseach agus tá mé ocrach.
examples.english: I am tired and I am hungry.

examples.irish: Ba mhaith liom dul, ach níl am agam.
examples.english: I would like to go, but I don't have time.

examples.irish: Nuair a tháinig sé, bhí áthas orainn.
examples.english: When he came, we were happy.

examples.irish: Sula mbeidh sé rómhall, caithfimid imeacht.
examples.english: Before it is too late, we must leave.

examples.irish: Cé go bhfuil sé fuar, téann sí amach.
examples.english: Although it is cold, she goes out.
If you are ready, we will start.

examples.irish: Dá mbeadh airgead agam, cheannóinn é.
examples.english: If I had money, I would buy it.

notes: Many learners confuse má (real/open condition, present/future) with dá (hypothetical/counterfactual). Má never eclipses; dá eclipses present/future verbs but lenites in the conditional.

title: Adverbs and Adverbial Phrases
summary: Most Irish adverbs of manner are formed with 'go' + adjective. Many common adverbs of time and place are fixed forms.
content:
MANNER ADVERBS — go + lenited adjective:
  go maith    — well
  go tapaidh  — quickly
  go mall     — slowly, late
  go luath    — soon, early
  go breá     — nicely, finely
  go ciúin    — quietly
  go láidir   — strongly

Before adjectives beginning with a vowel, go adds h-:
  go hálainn  — beautifully
  go héasca   — easily
  go hoscailte — openly

TIME ADVERBS (fixed forms):
  anois    — now
  arís     — again
  cheana   — already
  fós      — still, yet
  riamh    — ever (in questions/negative); never (with ní)
  i gcónaí — always
  uaireanta — sometimes
  go minic  — often
  ó shin    — since then, ago
  inné     — yesterday
  amárach  — tomorrow

PLACE ADVERBS:
  anseo  — here (position)
  ansin  — there (position)
  ansiúd — over there
  isteach — into (motion inward)
  amach  — out (motion outward)
  suas   — up (motion)
  síos   — down (motion)
  thuas  — up (position)
  thíos  — down (position)

ADVERBIAL PHRASES with prepositions:
  ar ball       — soon, in a while
  faoi láthair  — at present, currently
  go fóill      — yet, for now
  i ndeireadh na dála — in the end, ultimately

examples.irish: Ní raibh mé riamh i Sasana.
Tá sí i gcónaí ag obair.

examples.english: I will be there soon / in a while.

notes: Direction adverbs (suas/síos, isteach/amach, anonn/anall) come in pairs: isteach (motion into) vs. istigh (position inside). Using the wrong one is a common learner error.

title: Ordinal Numbers (Uimhreacha Orduiúla)
summary: Ordinal numbers in Irish use a definite article + prefix form. The first few are irregular.
content:
ORDINAL NUMBERS:
  1st  — an chéad (+ lenition of noun)
  2nd  — an dara / an darna
  3rd  — an tríú
  4th  — an ceathrú
  5th  — an cúigiú
  6th  — an séú
  7th  — an seachtú
  8th  — an t-ochtú
  9th  — an naoú
  10th — an deichiú

For 11th–19th, add déag:
  11th — an t-aonú ... déag
  12th — an dóú ... déag
  20th — an fichiú

USAGE:
  an chéad + lenited noun: an chéad lá (the first day)
  From 2nd onward: ordinal + noun in genitive or plain form depending on context:
    an dara lá     (the second day)
    an tríú háit   (third place)
    an ceathrú rann (the fourth verse)

FRACTIONS share these forms:
  leath   — half
  trian   — a third
  ceathrú — a quarter (same as 4th)
  cúigiú  — a fifth

examples.english: the fourth part of the book
next Thursday (lit. the first next Thursday)

notes: An chéad always lenites the following noun (if lenitable). From an dara onward, no lenition. The ordinal comes before the noun, unlike cardinal numbers which follow: trí cinn (three of them) vs. an tríú ceann (the third one).

title: Compound Prepositions (Réamhfhocail Chomhshuite)
summary: Compound prepositions are multi-word phrases that govern the genitive case of the following noun.
content:
Compound prepositions consist of a simple preposition + noun (sometimes + another preposition). The noun following a compound preposition is in the GENITIVE case.

COMMON COMPOUND PREPOSITIONS:
  ar aghaidh    — in front of, facing, ahead
  os comhair    — in front of, opposite (with genitive)
  i ndiaidh     — after, behind, following
  in aice (le)  — beside, near
  le linn       — during, at the time of
  de réir        — according to
  in ionad       — instead of
  i gcaitheamh  — throughout, during
  ar son         — for the sake of, for
  ar feadh       — for (duration of time)
  i lár          — in the middle of
  thar ceann    — on behalf of
  faoi dhéin    — towards, to meet

When followed by a PRONOUN, compound prepositions use prepositional pronouns on the first element:
  ar mo aghaidh → i mo dhiaidh → lena linn → dá réir
  (my/their/his portion absorbed into first prep)

Most commonly:
  ina dhiaidh sin  — after that
  dá réir sin      — accordingly, as a result
  ina theannta sin — in addition to that

examples.irish: Sheas sé os comhair an tí.
examples.english: He stood in front of the house.

examples.irish: Tháinig sí i ndiaidh an bhéile.
Le linn an chogaidh, bhí sé deacair.
examples.english: During the war, it was difficult.

examples.irish: De réir an dlí, tá sé mídhleathach.
examples.english: According to the law, it is illegal.

examples.irish: In ionad caife, d'ól mé tae.
examples.english: Instead of coffee, I drank tea.

notes: The genitive after compound prepositions is a common point of error. Remember that definite nouns take the genitive article (an → na for feminine, na → na for plural). When the object is a pronoun, compound prepositions have their own inflected forms.

title: The Past Tense (Aimsir Chaite)
summary: The Irish past tense lenites the verb stem (or adds d' before vowels). Endings are minimal — person is usually shown by pronoun.
content:
FORMATION — 1st Conjugation (monosyllabic stems):
  Lenite initial consonant (or add d' before vowels/fh-):
  bris → bhris mé  (I broke)
  ól  → d'ól mé   (I drank)
  fan → d'fhan mé  (I waited)
  glan → ghlan mé  (I cleaned)

1st Conjugation synthetic (ending carries person):
  1sg:  bhris-eamar / ghlan-amar  (we broke / cleaned) [1pl synthetic]
  All other persons use pronoun + base past form.

2nd Conjugation (polysyllabic, -igh/-aigh stems):
  ceannaigh → cheannaigh mé  (I bought)
  imigh    → d'imigh mé     (I left)
  éirigh   → d'éirigh mé    (I got up)
  lean follows 1st conj pattern despite ending: lean → lean mé

NEGATIVE — ní + lenition:
  Níor bhris mé é.    (I didn't break it.)
  Níor cheannaigh sí. (She didn't buy.)
  Níor ól mé é.       (I didn't drink it.) — 'níor' before vowels and fh

QUESTION — ar + lenition (past particle):
  Ar bhris tú é?      (Did you break it?)
  Ar cheannaigh tú?   (Did you buy?)
  Ar ól tú é?         (Did you drink it?)

KEY IRREGULAR PAST FORMS:
  téigh → chuaigh     (went)
  tar   → tháinig     (came)
  abair → dúirt       (said)
  bí    → bhí         (was)
  déan  → rinne       (did/made)
  faigh → fuair       (got)
  feic  → chonaic     (saw)
  ith   → d'ith       (ate)
  clois → chuala      (heard)
  tabhair → thug      (gave)
  beir  → rug         (caught, gave birth)

examples.irish: Ar chuala tú an scéal? — Chuala.
examples.english: Did you hear the news? — Yes.

examples.irish: Rinne sí an obair go maith.

notes: The past tense particle in dependent position is 'ar' (leniting), not 'a'. In Ulster Irish, 'cha' / 'chan' replaces 'ní / níor' in many negative contexts. The 1pl synthetic form '-amar/-eamar' is used in formal and written Irish; colloquially, 'muid/sinn' is added to the 3sg form.

title: Advanced Copula Constructions
summary: The copula changes form across tenses and clause types. Mastering gur/gurb, ba/b', and double-copula structures is essential at C1.
content:
TENSE FORMS OF THE COPULA:
  Present:    is (positive), ní (negative), an? (question), nach? (neg. question)
  Past/Cond:  ba / b' (positive), níorbh / níor (negative), arbh / ar? (question)
  Subordinate present:  gur / gurb (that it is), nach (that it is not)
  Subordinate past:     gurbh / gur (that it was), nárbh / nár

b' is used before vowels and fh- in past/conditional:
  b'fhearr liom tae.  (I preferred tea.)
  Ba bhreá liom é.    (I would love it.)

DOUBLE COPULA — emphasis or classification of a modified noun:
  Is é an rud is mó a bhíonn deacair.  (It is the biggest thing that tends to be difficult.)
  Is é Seán is fearr.  (It's Seán who is best.)
  Ba é an lá ba fhearr é.  (It was the best day.)

COPULA IN SUBORDINATE CLAUSES:
  Deir sí gur múinteoir é.      (She says he is a teacher.)
  Cheap mé gurbh amhlaidh é.    (I thought that was so.)
  Dúirt sé nárbh é a thuairim.  (He said it wasn't his opinion.)

IS EA / NÍ HEA (standard yes/no for copula questions):
  An dochtúir thú? — Is ea. / Ní hea.

COPULA + ADJECTIVE PREDICATE (formal/literary pattern):
  Is maith an rud é.   (It is a good thing.)
  Is mór an trua é.    (It is a great pity.)
  Ba mhóide an brón é. (It added to the sorrow.)

notes: The choice between gur and gurb before vowels parallels is/is (is before consonants, is before vowels). Arbh / níorbh are used before vowels and fh- in past questions/negatives. These distinctions matter in careful writing but are often collapsed in speech.

title: Preverbal Particles and Dependent Forms
summary: Every Irish verb clause has a particle (or lacks one) that determines its meaning and the mutation it triggers. These particles must be matched to the correct dependent verb form.
content:
Irish verbs have two sets of forms: INDEPENDENT (used in main affirmative clauses, no particle) and DEPENDENT (used after all particles).

PARTICLES AND THEIR MUTATIONS:

Main clause:
  [none]    — affirmative, independent form: Téim. Chuaigh sí.
  ní        — negative, lenition: Ní théim. Ní chuaigh sí.
  an?       — question, eclipsis: An dtéann tú? An ndeachaigh sí?
  nach?     — negative question, eclipsis: Nach dtéann tú?

Past tense (special particles):
  níor      — negative past, lenition: Níor tháinig sé.
  ar?       — question past, lenition: Ar tháinig sí?
  nár?      — negative question past, lenition: Nár tháinig sé?

Subordinate / reported:
  go        — 'that' (affirmative, present/future), eclipsis: Deir sí go dtagann sé.
  gur/gurb  — 'that' (past/conditional), lenition: Cheap sé gur tháinig sí.
  nach       — 'that...not', eclipsis: Deir sé nach dtagann sé.
  nár        — 'that...not' (past/conditional), lenition: Cheap sé nár tháinig sí.

Conditional/temporal conjunctions also use these:
  nuair a   — lenition (when)
  sula      — eclipsis (before)
  má        — lenition (if, real)
  dá        — eclipsis/conditional form (if, hypothetical)

NOTE ON BÍ: Bí has special dependent forms:
  an mbíonn? nach mbíonn? go mbíonn — present habitual
  an raibh? nach raibh? go raibh    — past
  an mbeidh? go mbeidh              — future

examples.english: I don't go home early. (ní + lenition)

examples.irish: Deir sí go dtagann sé i gcónaí.
examples.english: She says he always comes. (go + eclipsis)
He didn't drink enough. (níor + lenition, past)
Didn't she tell you? (nár + lenition, past neg. question)

notes: The irregular verbs bí, téigh, tar, abair, déan, faigh, feic, clois, tabhair, beir, ith have irregular dependent forms — especially in past tense. These must be learned individually. A key confusion point: 'go' (the conjunction 'that') triggers eclipsis, but 'nuair a' (when) triggers lenition.

title: The Genitive with Verbal Nouns
summary: When a verbal noun takes a definite object, that object goes into the genitive case — a key structural difference from English.
content:
In Irish, the verbal noun (VN) functions like a noun. When it has an object:

INDEFINITE OBJECT — stays in nominative after VN:
  ag scríobh litreach   — writing a letter
  ag léamh leabhair     — reading a book (partitive genitive; see note)
  ag ithe aráin         — eating bread (indefinite)

DEFINITE OBJECT — goes into genitive before VN in a nominal context, OR appears with object pronoun:
  ag scríobh na litreach  — writing the letter (genitive with article)
  ag léamh an leabhair    — reading the book (genitive)
  á scríobh               — writing it (object pronoun replaces noun: á = ag + a)

VERBAL NOUN AS SUBJECT OR COMPLEMENT:
  Is maith liom snámh.      — I like swimming. (VN as object of 'is maith liom')
  Tá snámh go maith aige.  — He swims well. (VN as subject)
  Thosaigh sí ag caint.    — She started talking. (VN after 'ag')

GENITIVE OF THE VN ITSELF:
  am codlata    — sleeping time, bedtime
  am léitheoireachta — reading time
  seomra folctha — bathroom (lit. room of bathing)
  lá oibre      — workday

OBJECT BEFORE VN (literary / emphatic):
  Chonaic mé ag scríobh litreach é.  — I saw him writing a letter.
  (object 'é' comes after the VN phrase in formal writing)

examples.irish: Tá mé ag léamh an leabhair.
examples.english: I am reading the book. (definite → genitive)
I am reading a book. (indefinite → nominative)

examples.irish: Tá sé ag scríobh na litreach.

notes: Indefinite objects of verbal nouns are actually in the genitive too (partitive), but for most nouns the partitive genitive is identical to the nominative. The definite genitive (with the article) is where the change becomes visible. The pronoun construction á (= ag + 3sg object) is the most common way to express a definite pronoun object of a verbal noun.

title: Discourse Markers and Sentence Connectors
summary: Discourse markers signal logical relationships between sentences — contrast, addition, result, concession. Essential for coherent written and spoken Irish.
content:
ADDITION:
  chomh maith (leis sin)  — also, as well (as that)
  thairis sin             — moreover, besides that
  ina theannta sin        — in addition to that, along with that
  anuas air sin           — on top of that, furthermore
  i dteannta a chéile     — together, combined

CONTRAST / CONCESSION:
  mar sin féin            — nonetheless, however, even so
  ach sin ráite           — that said
  cé sin                  — although, even though (literary)
  ar an láimh eile        — on the other hand
  in ainneoin sin         — despite that, in spite of that

RESULT / CONSEQUENCE:
  mar sin                 — so, therefore
  dá bharr sin            — as a result of that, consequently
  ar an gcaoi sin         — in that way, accordingly
  dá réir sin             — accordingly, correspondingly
  uime sin                — therefore (formal/literary)

CLARIFICATION / EMPHASIS:
  ar ndóigh               — of course, naturally
  go deimhin              — indeed, certainly
  i ndáiríre              — really, truly, in fact
  is é sin le rá          — that is to say
  is é sin                — namely, that is

TIME / SEQUENCE:
  ar dtús                 — first, at first
  ina dhiaidh sin         — after that, subsequently
  faoi dheireadh          — finally, at last
  idir an dá linn         — meanwhile, in the meantime
  ó shin i leith          — since then

Ar dtús, lean siad an treoracha. Ina dhiaidh sin, rinne siad a rogha rud féin.
examples.english: At first, they followed the instructions. After that, they did their own thing.

examples.irish: Thairis sin, caithfear smaoineamh ar an gcostas.
examples.english: Moreover, one must think about the cost.

examples.english: That is to say, there was no other option.

notes: Many of these markers are prepositional phrases with demonstratives (sin 'that'). They typically come clause-initially and are often set off by a comma. In formal registers, uime sin and dá réir sin are preferred; in speech, mar sin and thairis sin are more common.

title: Literary and Archaic Verb Forms
summary: Classical and literary Irish uses synthetic verb endings, older autonomous forms, and second-person singular distinctions not found in the standard.
content:
SYNTHETIC ENDINGS (person encoded in the verb, not a separate pronoun):
Modern standard prefers analytic (verb + pronoun), but literary and formal texts use synthetic forms:

  Present:
    1sg: -aim/-im    (deirim — I say)   vs. analytic: deir mé
    1pl: -imid/-aimid (deirimid — we say) vs. deir muid
    2sg: -ir (deir tú — no synthetic in most modern verbs; older: deirir)

  Past:
    1pl: -amar/-eamar (chuamar — we went) vs. chuaigh muid

  Future:
    1sg: -fad/-fead  (rachad — I will go) vs. rachaidh mé
    1pl: -faimid     (rachaimid — we will go)

  Conditional:
    1sg: -fainn      (rachainn — I would go)
    2sg: -fá         (rachfá — you would go)
    1pl: -faimis     (rachaimis)

ARCHAIC AUTONOMOUS (passive-like) FORMS:
  The standard autonomous uses -tear/-tar (present) and -adh/-eadh (past).
  Older texts show: -thear (present lenited), and -thas (past, from -(e)adh):
    Rinneadh é.   — Standard: It was done.
    Rinnteas é.   — Older/dialectal variant.

2nd PERSON SINGULAR (tú vs. thú):
  In literary Irish, 'thú' is the object form and 'tú' the subject.
  Standard Irish uses 'tú' for both, but literature preserves the distinction:
    Chonaic mé thú. (I saw you.) — object
    Tháinig tú.     (You came.)  — subject

PAST COPULA IN LITERARY USE:
  Ba + lenition in elaborate nominal sentences:
    Ba mhian leis dul ann.  (He wished/desired to go there.)
    Ba mhór an crá croí é. (It was a great heartache.)

I will go there tomorrow. (1sg future synthetic)
I would go if I had time. (1sg conditional)

The work was done well. (standard autonomous past)

notes: The synthetic forms are not merely archaic — they survive in all dialects to varying degrees. Munster Irish is especially synthetic. Reading any 20th-century prose or poetry requires comfort with 1sg -aim, 1pl -imid/-(a)mar, and the conditional endings. The tú/thú distinction appears throughout Peig, An tOileánach, and other canonical texts.

title: Classical vs. Standard Spelling
summary: Pre-standard Irish texts use older spelling conventions. Recognising classical orthographic patterns is essential for reading literature printed before the 1950s.
content:
The Caighdeán Oifigiúil (Official Standard) was introduced in 1958 and revised in 2017. Texts before this — and many literary works in dialect — use older spelling.

KEY DIFFERENCES:

1. SILENT LETTERS — classical Irish retains etymological letters now silent or removed:
   Classical: tighe (of a house) → Standard: tí
   Classical: oidhche → Standard: oíche  (night)
   Classical: cneidh → Standard: cneá  (wound)
   Classical: aoidh → Standard: aí (guest)

2. DIPHTHONG SPELLINGS:
   Classical: gníomh, snámh, biadh, tigh
   Standard:  gníomh (same), snámh (same), bia, teach (declension simplified)

3. GENITIVE FORMS — classical uses fuller vowel in genitive:
   Classical: leabhair (of a book, 2 syllables clearly)
   Standard:  leabhair (same, but other forms more compressed)
   Classical feminine genitives often retained: na mná (standard same)

4. ECLIPSIS SPELLING — pre-standard texts sometimes wrote both letters in full:
   Classical: i bpeann (in a pen) — same as standard
   But older texts: 'i bh-fearann' with hyphen for eclipsis

5. VERBAL FORMS — older endings preserved:
   Classical: do chuaidh → Standard: chuaigh  (went)
   Classical: do rinne   → Standard: rinne    (did)
   The particle 'do/d'' before past tense was obligatory in older writing.

6. THE PARTICLE 'DO' (past tense marker):
   Classical texts always write: Do chuaigh sé. Do dúirt sí.
   Standard: drops 'do' — Chuaigh sé. Dúirt sí.
   'D'' survives before vowels and fh- in the standard.

7. DIALECT SPELLINGS:
   Munster literary tradition: bheith (to be — Munster spelling of bheith, same actually)
   Connacht: síol, fíor (same), but vowel syncope spelling varies
   Ulster: spellings closer to Scottish Gaelic in some older texts

examples.english: He went to Dublin. (classical form with 'do' particle)

examples.english: He was sitting at the foot of the house. (tighe = classical genitive of teach)
throughout the night (oidhche = classical spelling of oíche)
She did her best. (do + past, classical)

the woman of the house (classical: tighe = genitive of teach)

notes: The particle 'do' is the single most immediately visible difference between classical and standard Irish. When reading Peig, An tOileánach, or Cré na Cille, expect 'do' before nearly every past tense verb. Once you recognise it as a past-tense marker that lenites the verb, classical texts become much more accessible.

title: Literary Register: Inversion, Fronting, and Poetic Word Order
summary: Literary Irish exploits VSO freedom for emphasis, topicalization, and rhythm. Recognising these patterns is key to reading poetry and formal prose.
content:
Irish VSO order is flexible. Literary and formal registers exploit this freedom for emphasis, rhythm, and topicalization.

TOPICALIZATION (fronting for emphasis):
Move the element you want to emphasize to the front, often as a cleft:
  Is san oíche a labhrann an chuach.  (It is at night that the cuckoo calls.)
  Is iad na daoine bochta is fearr a thuigeann é.  (It is the poor people who understand it best.)

ADVERBIAL FRONTING — placing time/place expressions before the verb:
  I dtús aimsire, ní raibh ach fiántas ann.  (In the beginning, there was only wilderness.)
  Ar maidin lá arna mhárach, d'éirigh sí.   (The morning of the next day, she rose.)

FRONTING OF OBJECT (literary, marked):
  An focal sin, ní déarfaidh mé choíche arís é.
  (That word — I will never say it again.)

POETIC INVERSION — adjective before noun (echoing older Irish):
  fada é an lá  (long is the day) — predicate-first, common in poetry
  Mairg nach bhfuil ina chailleach.  (Woe to one who is not an old woman — literary)

APPOSITION AND ELABORATION:
  Literary prose often delays the main verb with long nominal expansions:
  An fear mór láidir a bhí ina chónaí ar imeall an bhaile, ba é a d'oscail an doras.
  (The big strong man who lived on the edge of the town — it was he who opened the door.)

ELLIPSIS — subject/object dropped when recoverable (more common in literature):
  Thóg sé an claiomh. Bhuail. Thit an namhaid.
  (He took the sword. Struck. The enemy fell.) — 'he' implied in 2nd/3rd verb.
