The VSO base order is highly amenable to fronting because the verb signals clause-start regardless; anything before the verb is therefore inherently marked/emphatic.

title: Broad and Slender: The Foundation of Irish Spelling
summary: Every Irish consonant is either broad (leathan) or slender (caol). This single principle underlies all Irish spelling and inflection.
content:
Every consonant in Irish is pronounced in one of two ways:
  BROAD (leathan) — adjacent to the vowels a, o, u
  SLENDER (caol)  — adjacent to the vowels e, i

Slender consonants are 'palatalized' — slightly 'y-coloured'. Broad consonants are not.
  bán (broad n) — sounds like English 'bawn'
  bín (slender n) — sounds like English 'been'

THE SPELLING RULE: Caol le caol, leathan le leathan
  ('Slender with slender, broad with broad')
  The vowels on BOTH SIDES of any consonant group must agree in quality.
  This is why endings are added the way they are — the added vowel must match the consonant's quality.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR INFLECTION:
  The genitive, plural, and verbal endings all insert or change vowels to satisfy this rule.
  fear (man) → genitive: fir  [the r becomes slender → insert i before r]
  bord (table) → genitive: boird  [d becomes slender → insert i]
  leabhar (book) → genitive: leabhair  [r becomes slender → insert i]
  lámh (hand) → genitive: láimhe  [mh becomes slender → insert i, add e]

IDENTIFYING BROAD vs. SLENDER:
  Look at the vowel(s) immediately beside the consonant(s):
  bord — o is beside d → d is broad
  boird — oi is beside d → d is slender (i makes it slender)
  scríobh —ío is beside bh → bh is slender (the i counts)
  scríobha — a is beside bh → bh turns broad (in this form)

CONSONANT GROUPS:
  In groups like 'bhr', 'str', 'gl', all consonants in the group share the same quality.
  The vowel on each side of the group determines the quality of the whole group.

examples.english: man / of a man (broad r → slender r)
table / of a table (broad d → slender d)
hand / of a hand (broad mh → slender mh + e)
white (adj) / plural/gen: broad n stays broad, add a

notes: This rule explains why Irish words sometimes look like they gain or lose vowels — the vowels are being inserted or adjusted to satisfy broad/slender agreement. Once you internalize this rule, Irish spelling becomes much more systematic. Dialects apply the rule consistently, but the specific quality of some consonants can vary.

title: The Imperative Mood (Modh Ordaitheach)
summary: The imperative is used for commands, requests, and suggestions. The 2sg form is simply the verb stem.
content:
The imperative has three forms in common use: 2sg (you), 1pl (let's), and 2pl (y'all).

2ND SINGULAR (talking to one person) = bare verb stem:
  1st conjugation: bris! (break!), glan! (clean!), ól! (drink!), fan! (wait!), ith! (eat!)
  2nd conjugation: ceannaigh! (buy!), imigh! (go/leave!), éirigh! (get up!)
  Note: the 2sg is the dictionary form — the simplest form of the verb.

1ST PLURAL (let's / we should) = stem + -imis (slender) / -aimis (broad):
  glan → glanaimis!   (let's clean!)
  bris → brisimis!    (let's break!)
  ól  → ólaímis!     (let's drink!)
  ceannaigh → ceannaimis!  (let's buy!)

2ND PLURAL (talking to a group) = stem + -igí (slender) / -aigí (broad):
  glan → glanaidí!... actually: glan + aigí = glanaigí!
  bris → brisigí!
  ól  → ólaigí!
  ceannaigh → ceannaigí!
  imigh → imígí!

NEGATIVE IMPERATIVE: ná + imperative form
  ná is not followed by lenition in the imperative
  ná adds h- before vowel-initial verbs:
  Ná glan é! (Don't clean it!)
  Ná bris é! (Don't break it!)
  Ná hith é! (Don't eat it!) — h before vowel
  Ná hól é! (Don't drink it!) — h before vowel
  Ná himigh! (Don't leave!) — h before vowel

POLITE REQUESTS — use the conditional instead:
  An gclánfá é sin? (Would you clean that?)
  An bhféadfá é sin a dhéanamh? (Could you do that?)
notes: Bí has irregular imperative forms: 2sg = bí!, 1pl = bímis!, 2pl = bígí! Negative: ná bí!, ná bímis!, ná bígí! The imperative of tabhair is tabhair (2sg), tugaigí (2pl). The imperative of abair is abair (2sg), abraigí (2pl).

title: Simple Prepositions: Meanings and Basic Use
summary: Irish has 15 simple prepositions. Each has a core meaning and a range of idiomatic uses. All inflect with pronouns.
content:
The 15 simple prepositions of Irish, with their core meanings:

  ag  — at, by; marks possession (tá x agam), progressive (ag léamh), and skills/states
  ar  — on, at, upon; marks many emotional states (tá áthas ar, tá ocras ar) and obligations
  as  — out of, from; origin from a place, made of a material
  chuig — to, towards; used for going to people, sending things to people
  de  — off, from, of; detachment or removal, some adjective idioms
  do  — to, for; indirect objects, benefit; also used in dative constructions
  faoi — under, about; under a surface, or concerning a topic; some emotional states
  i/in — in, into; location inside something (i eclipses following noun)
  idir — between; requires two entities or a plural
  le  — with, by; accompaniment, agreement, connection, ownership idioms
  ó   — from, since; separation from a person or place, origin, time since
  roimh — before, in front of; temporal (before an event) or physical (in front of)
  thar — over, past, beyond; motion across or beyond something
  trí  — through; motion or passage through something
  um  — about, around; used mainly in set phrases (um Nollaig = around Christmas)

KEY DISTINCTIONS:
  go (to a place) vs. chuig (to a person):
    Tá mé ag dul go Gaillimh.  (I'm going to Galway — place)
    Tá mé ag dul chuig mo chara.  (I'm going to my friend — person)

  ó (from — origin/separation) vs. as (from — out of):
    Is as Corcaigh mé.  (I'm from Cork — origin, as is idiomatic here)
    Tháinig sé ó Mháire.  (It came from Máire — from a person)
    Tháinig sé as an mbosca.  (It came out of the box — emergence)

  do (for/to) vs. le (with/for in some senses):
    Cheannaigh mé é do Sheán.  (I bought it for Seán — beneficiary)
    Tá sé le hÁine.  (It is with/belongs to Áine — possession idiom)

examples.english: I sent a letter to her. (chuig = to a person)

examples.irish: Tá sé faoi bhun na fuinneoige.
examples.english: It is under the window. (faoi = under)
He went over the bridge. (thar = over/past)
She was before him / ahead of him. (roimh = before)

notes: All simple prepositions have inflected forms when followed by a pronoun — these are the prepositional pronouns (see that card). When followed by the definite article, most prepositions contract: ag an → ag an (no change), ar an → ar an (no change), but i + an → sa/san, de + an → den, do + an → don, etc.

title: The h-Prefix and t-Prefix
summary: Besides lenition and eclipsis, Irish has two more initial changes: the h-prefix (before vowels in specific grammatical environments) and the t-prefix (masculine nouns after 'an').
content:
Irish has four types of initial changes. Lenition and eclipsis are the most common, but h-prefixing and t-prefixing are equally systematic.

H-PREFIX — added before vowel-initial words in these environments:

1. After 3sg FEMININE possessive 'a' (her):
   a hata     (her hat)    a héadan   (her face)
   a hainm    (her name)   a hathair  (her father)
   Compare: a (his) + vowel → lenition or d': a éadan → a éadan (no change — 3sg masc possessive doesn't trigger h)

2. After 'go' + adjective (degree adverb):
   go hálainn    (beautifully)   go hiontach  (wonderfully)
   go healaíonta (artistically)  go héasca    (easily)

3. After definite article 'na' (nom plural / gen sg feminine) before vowels:
   na héin        (the birds)     na húlla       (the apples)
   na háiteanna   (the places)    na hÉireannach (the Irish people)

T-PREFIX — added before certain vowel-initial nouns:

1. MASCULINE nouns after 'an' (nominative singular) beginning with a vowel:
   an t-arán   (the bread)    an t-uisce  (the water)
   an t-am     (the time)     an t-éan    (the bird)
   an t-ainm   (the name)     an t-im     (the butter)

2. FEMININE nouns after 'an' (nominative singular) beginning with sl-, sn-, sr-:
   an tsráid   (the street)   an tsrón    (the nose)
   an tsnámh   (the swimming) an tslí     (the way/path)

T-PREFIX is NOT used:
   In the genitive of masculine vowel-initial nouns: an éin (of the bird — no t-)
   After other prepositions: ar an arán (not *ar an t-arán — wait, actually yes: ar an arán eclipses)
   With feminine nouns beginning with s + other consonants: an scoil (no t-, scoil is feminine)

IMPORTANT: After 'ar an', 'ag an', 'leis an' etc., the standard uses eclipsis (not t-prefix):
   ar an mbord, ag an doras — the t-prefix rule only applies directly after the bare article 'an'.

examples.irish: Cad is ainm di? — Áine is ainm di. Cad is ainm dá hathair?
examples.english: What is her name? — Áine. What is her father's name? (h-prefix on hathair)
The water is cold. (t-prefix on uisce)
The birds are singing. (h-prefix after na)
The street is crowded. (t-prefix on feminine sráid)
the bread and the butter (t-prefix on both)

notes: A useful memory aid: the h-prefix 'softens' the transition to a vowel (adds a consonant before the vowel). The t-prefix 'hardens' the start of a word (replaces the vowel onset with a dental stop). Both are written with a hyphen: an t-uisce, go hálainn (no hyphen for h-prefix in standard).

title: Days, Months, Seasons, and Dates
summary: Calendar vocabulary in Irish comes with specific grammatical structures: days use 'Dé' for 'on', months use 'i mí', and seasons use 'sa/san'.
content:
DAYS OF THE WEEK (Laethanta na Seachtaine):
  Dé Luain     — Monday
  Dé Máirt     — Tuesday
  Dé Céadaoin  — Wednesday
  Déardaoin    — Thursday (note: no 'Dé' prefix)
  Dé hAoine    — Friday (h-prefix: Aoine → hAoine)
  Dé Sathairn  — Saturday
  Dé Domhnaigh — Sunday

'ON' A DAY OF THE WEEK: use 'Dé' alone (no extra preposition needed):
  Dé Luain     — on Monday
  Dé Sathairn  — on Saturday
  But: 'Ar an' + day name is also used in speech: ar an Luan, ar an Satharn

LAST / NEXT:
  Dé Luain seo caite   — last Monday
  Dé Luain seo chugainn — next Monday

MONTHS (Míonna na Bliana):
  Eanáir, Feabhra, Márta, Aibreán, Bealtaine, Meitheamh
  Iúil, Lúnasa, Meán Fómhair, Deireadh Fómhair, Samhain, Nollaig

'IN' A MONTH: i mí + month name:
  i mí Eanáir   (in January)    i mí Iúil     (in July)
  i mí na Nollag (in December — Nollaig → na Nollag in genitive)

SEASONS (Séasúir):
  an t-earrach (spring)   san earrach  (in spring)
  an samhradh  (summer)   sa samhradh  (in summer)
  an fómhar    (autumn)   sa bhfómhar / san fhómhar (in autumn)
  an geimhreadh (winter)  sa gheimhreadh (in winter)

YEARS:
  i mbliana     — this year
  anuraidh      — last year
  an bhliain seo chugainn — next year
  In specific years: sa bhliain dhá mhíle is... (in the year 2000s...)

DATE EXPRESSIONS:
  An chéad lá de mhí Eanáir  — the 1st of January
  An dara lá déag de mhí Mhárta — the 12th of March
  Cén lá den mhí é? — What day of the month is it?
  Is é an (ordinal) lá de mhí (month) é — It is the Xth of (month).

examples.irish: Dé Luain seo caite, d'imigh sí.
An chéad lá de mhí na Nollag
Tagann na cuacha i mí Aibreáin.

notes: Note that Irish months are not capitalized (unlike English). Déardaoin (Thursday) is irregular — it does not take the 'Dé' prefix. Dé hAoine takes the h-prefix because Aoine is vowel-initial. In Ulster Irish, the days often use different forms.

title: The Future Tense (Aimsir Fháistineach)
summary: The future tense uses the endings -faidh/-fidh (1st conjugation) and -óidh/-eoidh (2nd conjugation). Key irregular futures must be learned.
content:
FORMATION — 1st Conjugation (monosyllabic stems):
  Broad stems → add -faidh:
  glan → glanfaidh  (will clean)
  ól  → ólfaidh    (will drink)
  fan → fanfaidh   (will wait)
  léigh → léifidh  (will read — slender)

  Slender stems → add -fidh:
  bris → brisfidh   (will break)
  buail → buailfidh (will hit)
  scríobh → scríobhfaidh (broad — scríobhfaidh)

2nd CONJUGATION (polysyllabic, -aigh/-igh stems):
  Broad: remove -aigh, add -óidh:
  ceannaigh → ceannóidh  (will buy)
  dúnaigh  → dúnóidh   (will close)

  Slender: remove -igh, add -eoidh:
  imigh   → imeoidh    (will leave)
  éirigh  → éireoidh   (will get up)
  bailigh → baileoidh  (will collect)

IRREGULAR FUTURES (must be learned):
  bí     → beidh       (will be)
  téigh  → rachaidh    (will go)
  tar    → tiocfaidh   (will come)
  abair  → déarfaidh   (will say)
  faigh  → gheobhaidh  (will get — highly irregular)
  feic   → feicfidh    (will see)
  clois  → cluinfidh   (will hear)
  tabhair → tabharfaidh (will give)
  beir   → béarfaidh   (will catch)
  ith    → íosfaidh    (will eat)
  déan   → déanfaidh   (will do/make — follows regular pattern)

NEGATIVE: ní + lenition:
  Ní rachaidh mé.    (I will not go.)
  Ní bheidh sé ann. (He will not be there.)
  Ní íosfaidh sí é. (She will not eat it.)

QUESTION: an + eclipsis:
  An rachaidh tú?      (Will you go?)
  An mbeidh tú ann?   (Will you be there?)
  An dtiocfaidh siad? (Will they come?)

SUBORDINATE: go + eclipsis:
  Deir sí go rachaidh sí.   (She says she will go.)
  Ceapann sé go mbeidh sé ann. (He thinks he will be there.)

examples.irish: Rachaidh mé go Baile Átha Cliath amárach.
examples.english: I will go to Dublin tomorrow.
She will come in a while.
They will buy a new house.
It will not be cold tomorrow.

examples.irish: Gheobhaidh tú é gan aon agó.
examples.english: You will get it without any doubt.

examples.irish: Déarfaidh sé an fhírinne, is dócha.
examples.english: He will tell the truth, probably.

notes: Gheobhaidh (from faigh, to get) is one of the most irregular futures in Irish — the stem changes completely. The future of déan is déanfaidh, which follows the regular 1st conjugation pattern. In Munster Irish, the 1sg future often uses synthetic -fad/-fead endings: raghad (I will go), tiocfad (I will come).

title: The Perfect Aspect: tar éis + Verbal Noun
summary: Irish expresses the perfect ('I have done X') using tá/bhí + tar éis + verbal noun. There is no separate perfect tense.
content:
Irish does not have a perfect tense (like English 'have done'). Instead, it uses the construction:
  tá/bhí + subject + tar éis + verbal noun

PRESENT PERFECT (something just done / recently completed):
  Tá mé tar éis é a dhéanamh.  (I have just done it. / I've done it.)
  Tá sí tar éis teacht.         (She has just come.)
  Tá siad tar éis imeacht.      (They have just left.)

PAST PERFECT (had done — use bhí):
  Bhí sé tar éis imeacht nuair a tháinig mé.  (He had already left when I came.)
  Bhí sí tar éis an leabhar a léamh.           (She had read the book.)

WHEN THE VERBAL NOUN HAS AN OBJECT:
  Put 'a' immediately before the verbal noun; the object comes BEFORE 'a':
  Tá mé tar éis an leabhar a léamh.    (I have just read the book.)
  Tá sé tar éis an dinnéar a ithe.     (He has just eaten the dinner.)
  Tá sí tar éis litir a scríobh.        (She has just written a letter.)

With a PRONOUN object, use á (= ag + 3sg object):
  Tá mé tar éis é a dhéanamh → Tá mé tar éis a dhéanamh  ... actually use:
  Tá mé tar éis é a chríochnú.  (I have just finished it.)

ALTERNATIVE: i ndiaidh (more common in Ulster and Connacht):
  Tá mé i ndiaidh é a dhéanamh.  (I have just done it.)
  This is equally valid and common in many dialects.

SIMPLE PAST vs. PERFECT:
  Rinne mé é.              — I did it. (simple past — action in the past)
  Tá mé tar éis é a dhéanamh. — I have just done it. (perfect — result in present)

examples.irish: Tá mé tar éis mo chuid oibre a chríochnú.
examples.english: I have just finished my work.

examples.irish: Tá sí tar éis dul a chodladh.
examples.english: She has just gone to sleep.

examples.irish: Bhí sé tar éis imeacht romhainn.
Tá mé tar éis an scannán sin a fheiceáil.
examples.english: I have just seen that film.

examples.irish: An bhfuil tú tar éis é sin a chloisteáil? — Táim.
examples.english: Have you just heard that? — Yes.

examples.irish: Tá siad tar éis teacht abhaile.
Tá mé i ndiaidh é a dhéanamh.
examples.english: I have just done it. (i ndiaidh variant)

notes: The construction 'tá X tar éis Y a dhéanamh' literally means 'X is after doing Y' — Irish expresses the perfect through a spatial metaphor (being after something). The 'a' before the verbal noun is a verbal particle, not the article. Do not confuse it with the possessive 'a' or the relative particle 'a'.

title: Personal Numbers (Uimhreacha Pearsanta)
summary: Irish uses a special set of numbers exclusively for counting people. Cardinal numbers are not used for people.
content:
When counting PEOPLE, Irish uses personal numbers — never cardinal numbers:

  beirt    — 2 people
  triúr    — 3 people
  ceathrar — 4 people
  cúigear  — 5 people
  seisear  — 6 people
  seachtar — 7 people
  ochtar   — 8 people
  naonúr   — 9 people
  deichniúr — 10 people

For 1 person: use duine amháin (one person) or aon duine.
For 11+: cardinal numbers + duine/daoine: aon duine dhéag (11), fiche duine (20).

USAGE — personal numbers + GENITIVE PLURAL of the noun:
  beirt mhac       (two sons — mac → genitive plural: mac; mutated: mhac)
  beirt iníonacha  (two daughters)
  triúr múinteoirí (three teachers)
  ceathrar ban     (four women — bean → genitive plural: ban)
  cúigear mac      (five sons)
  seisear fear     (six men — fear → genitive plural: fear)

STANDING ALONE (without a noun):
  Bhí beirt ann.         (There were two people there.)
  Tháinig triúr.         (Three people came.)
  Cé mhéad duine? — Seisear. (How many people? — Six.)

DECLINATION — personal numbers decline like nouns:
  leis an mbeirt    (with the two of them)
  don triúr         (for the three of them)
  ag an gceathrar   (at the four of them)

PRONOUNS after personal numbers:
  Personal numbers typically refer to mixed or male groups.
  For female groups, the same numbers are used.
  beirt (the two of them) is common as a standalone pronoun-like form.

examples.english: There were seven of us there.

examples.irish: Deichniúr ban a bhí sa ghrúpa.
examples.english: There were ten women in the group.
The two of them left. (beirt with definite article)

notes: The personal numbers are one of the most distinctly Irish features of the language. Never say *dhá dhuine* for 'two people' — say *beirt*. The distinction between personal and cardinal numbers is strictly observed by native speakers. Note that beirt, when definite, becomes an bheirt (lenited after the article, as it is feminine in grammatical gender).

title: The Conditional Tense (Modh Coinníollach): Forms
summary: The conditional expresses 'would'. It is built on the future stem with past-style endings. All forms have initial lenition (or d' before vowels).
content:
The conditional always begins with a lenited (or d'-prefixed) verb — this is how you know it's conditional.

1ST CONJUGATION — BROAD STEMS (add -fadh for 3sg, -fainn for 1sg, etc.):
  glan (clean):   ghlanfainn, ghlanfá, ghlanfadh, ghlanfaimis, ghlanfadh sibh, ghlanfaidís
  ól  (drink):    d'ólfainn, d'ólfá, d'ólfadh, d'ólfaimis, d'ólfadh sibh, d'ólfaidís
  fan (wait):     d'fhanfainn, d'fhanfá, d'fhanfadh

1ST CONJUGATION — SLENDER STEMS (add -feadh/-finn/-feá etc.):
  bris (break):   bhrisfinn, bhrisfea, bhrisfeadh, bhrisfimis, bhrisfeadh sibh, bhrisfidís
  léigh (read):   léifinn, léifeá, léifeadh, léifimis

2ND CONJUGATION — BROAD (-óinn/-ódh):
  ceannaigh:      cheannóinn, cheannófá, cheannódh, cheannóimis, cheannódh sibh, cheannóidís
  dúnaigh:        dhúnóinn, dhúnódh

2ND CONJUGATION — SLENDER (-eoinn/-eodh):
  imigh:          d'imeoinn, d'imeofá, d'imeodh, d'imeoimis
  éirigh:         d'éireoinn, d'éireodh

IRREGULAR CONDITIONAL FORMS:
  bí:       bheinn, bheifá, bheadh, bheimis, bheadh sibh, bheidís
  téigh:    rachainn, rachfá, rachadh, rachaimis, rachadh sibh, rachaidís
  tar:      thiocfainn, thiocfá, thiocfadh, thiocfaimis
  abair:    déarfainn, déarfá, déarfadh
  faigh:    gheobhainn, gheofá, gheobhadh, gheobhaimis
  feic:     d'fheicfinn, d'fheicfeá, d'fheicfeadh
  clois:    chluinfinn, chluinfeadh
  tabhair:  thabharfainn, thabharfadh
  ith:      d'íosfainn, d'íosfadh
  déan:     dhéanfainn, dhéanfadh
  beir:     bhéarfainn, bhéarfadh

NEGATIVE: ní + lenition (conditional verb already lenited — ní adds nothing new):
  Ní rachainn ann.  (I would not go there.)
  Ní bheadh sé ann. (He would not be there.)

QUESTION: an + eclipsis:
  An rachadh sí?     (Would she go?)
  An mbeadh tú ann? (Would you be there?)

examples.irish: Rachainn ann dá mbeadh am agam.
examples.english: I would go there if I had time.

examples.irish: Cheannódh sé é dá mbeadh airgead aige.
examples.english: He would buy it if he had money.
I would be happy. (lit. happiness would be on me)

examples.irish: Ní thiocfainn ar ais go deo.

examples.english: Would you do gardening? — I would.
I would get it if I asked.
I would eat anything right now.

notes: The conditional personal endings are: -inn (1sg), -fá/-feá (2sg), -fadh/-feadh (3sg), -faimis/-fimis (1pl), -fadh/-feadh sibh (2pl), -faidís/-fidís (3pl). The 2sg -fá/-feá is distinctive and common in speech. The conditional of bí (bheadh/bheinn) is especially high-frequency and must be automatic.

title: The Five Noun Declensions
summary: Irish nouns belong to one of five declensions, which determine how the genitive and plural are formed. Recognising a noun's declension is key to correct inflection.
content:
Irish nouns are grouped into 5 declensions. The declension predicts the genitive singular and often the plural.

1ST DECLENSION — mostly masculine, ends in broad consonant:
  Genitive: slenderize final consonant (insert -i- if needed for caol le caol)
  Plural: often same as genitive (or + -a in some subgroups)
  Examples: fear/fir, bord/boird, leabhar/leabhair, cat/cait, bád/báid, ceol/ceoil
  Plural: fir (men), boird (tables), leabhair (books)

2ND DECLENSION — mostly feminine, varied endings:
  Genitive: slenderize + add -e (slender) or -a (broad endings, e.g. -óg → -óige)
  Plural: usually + -a
  Examples:
    lámh → láimhe (hand); plural: lámha
    cloch → cloiche (stone); plural: clocha
    fuinneog → fuinneoige (window); plural: fuinneoga
    scoil → scoile (school); plural: scoileanna
    bean → mná (woman — highly irregular); plural: mná

3RD DECLENSION — mixed gender, varied:
  Genitive: often + -(e)ach or -(a)igh — or the stem changes
  Many verbal nouns and abstract nouns belong here
  Examples:
    sagart → sagairt (priest); plural: sagairt
    eochair → eochrach (key); plural: eochracha
    triail → trialach (trial); plural: trialacha
    súil → súl (eye — irregular); plural: súile

4TH DECLENSION — mixed, genitive = nominative (no change):
  The genitive is the same form as the nominative — the easiest declension
  Includes most verbal nouns, loanwords, nouns ending in a vowel
  Examples:
    bia → bia (food — gen = nom)
    dlí → dlí (law)
    rí → rí (king); plural: ríthe
    léamh → léamh (reading — verbal noun)
    scríobh → scríobh (writing — verbal noun)
    baile → baile (town); plural: bailte

5TH DECLENSION — mostly feminine, various:
  Genitive: often -(e)ach or adding -d, various patterns
  Examples:
    caora → caorach (sheep); plural: caoirigh
    cathair → cathrach (city); plural: cathracha
    abhainn → abhann (river); plural: aibhneacha
    comharsa → comharsan (neighbour); plural: comharsana
    traein → traenach (train); plural: traenacha

examples.english: the big man's house (1st declension: fear → fir)
the top of the hand (2nd declension: lámh → láimhe)
the key of the door (3rd declension: eochair → eochrach... actually: eochair → eochrach is gen. but 'dorais' is gen. of doras, 1st decl)
reading time (4th declension: léamh gen = léamh)
the bank of the river (5th declension: abhainn → abhann)
keeping the sheep (5th declension: caora → caorach, with eclipsis na g-)

notes: In practice, you learn a noun's declension by learning the genitive form alongside the nominative — dictionaries always list both. A useful heuristic: if the noun ends in a broad consonant and is masculine, it's likely 1st declension. If it ends in -óg/-eog/-lann and is feminine, it's likely 2nd. Verbal nouns are 4th. When in doubt, check a dictionary.

title: Indirect and Embedded Questions
summary: Indirect questions embed a question inside a statement or another question. The question word introduces a dependent clause with the verb in its dependent (lenited) form.
content:
An INDIRECT (embedded) question reports or contains a question without asking it directly.
Direct:   Cá bhfuil sé? (Where is he?)
Indirect: Ní fhios dom cá bhfuil sé. (I don't know where he is.)

COMMON QUESTION WORDS IN INDIRECT QUESTIONS:
  cé     — who:        Ní fhios dom cé a bhí ann.
  cad/céard — what:   D'fhiafraigh sí céard a tharla.
  cá     — where:     Ní thuigim cá bhfuil sé.
  cathain — when:     Ní fhios dom cathain a thiocfaidh sé.
  cén fáth — why:     Níl a fhios agam cén fáth ar ith sé é.
  conas/cén chaoi — how: D'inis sé conas a rinne sé é.
  cé mhéad — how many: Ní fhios dom cé mhéad a chosnaíonn sé.
  cén — which/what:  Fiafraigh di cén leabhar a mhol sí.

THE VERB after the question word: uses the DIRECT RELATIVE form (usually lenition where applicable):
  Ní fhios dom cé a rinne é. (I don't know who did it.) [rinne — lenited past]
  Dúirt sí cén áit ar chónaigh sí. (She said which place she lived.)

YES/NO INDIRECT QUESTIONS — use 'an' (eclipsis) or 'cé acu':
  Ní fhios dom an mbeidh sé ann. (I don't know if he'll be there.)
  Fiafraigh de an dtiocfaidh sí. (Ask him whether she will come.)
  Ní cinnte dom an raibh sí ann. (I'm not sure if she was there.)

NEGATIVE INDIRECT QUESTIONS — use 'nach':
  Ní fhios dom nach bhfuil sé ann. (I don't know that he's not there.)

USEFUL PHRASES for indirect questions:
  Ní fhios dom...          — I don't know...
  Níl a fhios agam...      — I don't know... (slightly different nuance)
  Níl mé cinnte...         — I'm not sure...
  D'fhiafraigh sé...       — He asked...
  Ní thuigim...            — I don't understand...
  Tá mé ag iarraidh a fháil amach... — I'm trying to find out...

examples.irish: Ní fhios dom cé a dúirt é.
examples.english: I don't know who said it.
She asked when I would come.

examples.irish: Ní thuigim cén fáth ar imigh sé.
examples.english: I don't understand why he left.

examples.irish: Ní fhios dom an mbeidh sé ann amárach.
examples.english: I don't know if he will be there tomorrow.

examples.irish: Innis dom conas a rinne tú é.
examples.english: Tell me how you did it.

examples.irish: Bhí mé ag iarraidh a fháil amach cá raibh sí.
examples.english: I was trying to find out where she was.

notes: The phrase 'ní fhios dom' (I don't know) is one of the most useful frames for indirect questions. Note 'ní fhios' — this is a special copula construction meaning 'it is not known'. Also note: 'cé' (who) and 'cad/céard' (what) are followed by 'a' + dependent verb; 'cá' (where) triggers eclipsis directly on the verb (cá bhfuil, cá raibh, cá mbeidh).

title: The Prospective Aspect: ar tí, chun, le + Verbal Noun
summary: Irish expresses intention and imminence through three constructions: ar tí (about to), chun (intending to/going to), and le + VN (to be done).
content:
Irish expresses different shades of future intention and imminence through verbal noun constructions. Together with the progressive (ag) and the perfect (tar éis), these form the Irish aspect system.

AR TÍ + verbal noun — about to (imminent, unplanned):
  Tá sé ar tí imeacht.      (He is about to leave.)
  Bhí sí ar tí titim.        (She was about to fall.)
  Tá an t-am ar tí a bheith suas. (The time is about to be up.)
  Ar tí implies something is on the verge of happening — not necessarily planned.

CHUN + verbal noun — intending to, going to, in order to (purposeful):
  Tá mé chun dul ann.              (I am going to go there. / I intend to go.)
  Tá sí chun an obair a chríochnú. (She is going to finish the work.)
  Chuaigh sé chun cainte léi.      (He went to talk to her — purpose.)
  Chun can express both intention and purpose (in order to).

LE + verbal noun — to be done, needing to be done (obligation/necessity):
  Tá an obair le déanamh.     (The work is to be done / needs to be done.)
  Bhí litir le scríobh aige.  (He had a letter to write.)
  Tá an bia le hullmhú.       (The food is to be prepared.)
  Tá teach le díol acu.       (They have a house to sell.)
  This construction is close in meaning to 'must be done' or 'needs to be done'.

COMBINED ASPECT SYSTEM overview:
  Progressive:   Tá sé ag obair.           (He is working — in progress)
  Perfect:       Tá sé tar éis oibriú.     (He has just worked — completed)
  Prospective:   Tá sé ar tí oibriú.       (He is about to work — imminent)
  Intentional:   Tá sé chun oibriú.        (He is going to work — planned)
  Obligatory:    Tá obair le déanamh aige. (He has work to do — due)

examples.irish: Bhí mé ar tí glaoch ort.
examples.english: I was about to call you.

examples.irish: Tá siad chun an teach a dhíol.
examples.english: They are going to sell the house.
There is plenty still to be done.

examples.irish: Chuaigh sí chun na cathrach chun siopadóireacht a dhéanamh.
examples.english: She went to the city in order to go shopping.

examples.irish: Bhí an traein ar tí imeacht nuair a shroich mé an stáisiún.
examples.english: The train was about to leave when I reached the station.

examples.irish: Tá litir le scríobh agam chuici.
examples.english: I have a letter to write to her.

notes: Ar tí and chun are often interchangeable in casual speech, but ar tí carries stronger imminence ('right now, at this moment') while chun carries intention ('I'm planning to'). The le + VN construction is close to the modal 'must' and is used in both personal obligation (Tá orm é a dhéanamh) and impersonal obligation (Tá sé le déanamh) contexts.

title: Syncopation in Polysyllabic Verb Stems
summary: Some polysyllabic verbs drop the vowel from their final syllable (syncopate) when adding personal endings. Recognising this pattern is essential for C1 reading.
content:
SYNCOPATION (sionacópáil) is the dropping of the unstressed final vowel of a polysyllabic verb stem when personal endings are added. It mainly affects 2nd conjugation verbs whose stems end in -(a)il, -(a)ir, -(a)in, -(a)is.

THE PATTERN:
  Dictionary form → syncopated stem (used with all tense endings except past 2sg/3sg)
  ceangail → ceangl-    (bind)
  oscail   → oscl-      (open)
  imir     → imr-       (play)
  inis     → ins-       (tell)
  coigil   → coigl-     (save, spare)
  foghlaim → foghla(i)m- (learn) — partial syncopation
  freastail → freastl-  (serve, attend)
  eitil    → eitl-      (fly)

HOW IT APPEARS IN EACH TENSE:
  PRESENT: syncopated stem + -ann/-eann
    ceangail: ceanglann (not *ceangailann)
    oscail:   osclaíonn (not *oscailíonn)
    imir:     imríonn   (not *imireann)
    inis:     insíonn   (not *iniseann)

  FUTURE: syncopated stem + -óidh/-eoidh
    ceangail: ceanglóidh
    oscail:   osclóidh
    imir:     imreoidh
    inis:     inseoidh

  CONDITIONAL: syncopated stem + -ódh/-eodh (3sg)
    ceangail: cheanghlódh (would bind)
    oscail:   d'osclódh   (would open)
    imir:     d'imreodh   (would play)

  PAST: NO syncopation — past uses the full dictionary form + lenition:
    ceangail → cheangail  (bound — no syncopation)
    oscail   → d'oscail   (opened — no syncopation)
    imir     → d'imir     (played — no syncopation)

  VERBAL NOUN: follows its own pattern (often not syncopated, or has different form)
    ceangail → ceangal (VN) or ceangailt
    oscail   → oscailt (VN)
    imir     → imirt   (VN)
    inis     → insint  (VN)

examples.english: He ties up a horse every morning. (syncopated: ceangl-)
They play a game every Saturday. (syncopated: imr-)
I will tell you about it. (syncopated future: ins-)

examples.irish: D'oscail sé an bosca. (no syncopation in past)

examples.english: It is playing football they are. (VN: imirt)

notes: The past tense never syncopates — this is the key exception. If you see 'd'oscail', 'cheangail', or 'd'imir', you are looking at a past tense form. If you see 'osclaíonn', 'ceanglann', 'imríonn' — syncopated, present tense. The verbal noun forms (oscailt, imirt, insint) must be learned individually as they follow their own conventions.

title: Defective and Restricted Verbs
summary: Several Irish verbs or verb-like constructions only appear in specific forms. Knowing these gaps prevents learners from constructing impossible forms.
content:
Some Irish constructions behave like verbs but are grammatically restricted — they only appear in certain tenses, persons, or forms.

COPULA-BASED 'MENTAL STATE' CONSTRUCTIONS:
These use the copula + adjective + preposition. They have no verbal noun and cannot be used progressively:
  is cuimhin le  — to remember:  Is cuimhin liom é. (I remember it.) Past: Ba chuimhin liom é.
  is eol do      — to know (a fact/place): Is eol dom cá bhfuil sé. Past: Ba eol dom.
  is col do      — to be related to: Is col ceathar dúinn iad. (They are our first cousins.)
  is oth le      — to regret, be sorry: Is oth liom sin. (I am sorry about that.) Past: Ba oth liom.
  is léir do     — to be clear to, to perceive: Is léir dom é. (It is clear to me.)
  is cuma le     — not to care: Is cuma liom. (I don't care.) Past: Ba chuma liom.
  is fiú         — to be worth: Is fiú é a dhéanamh. (It's worth doing.)

THE QUOTATIVE 'ARSA' (said — in direct speech):
  arsa is used ONLY for attributing direct speech in the past tense. It cannot be conjugated:
  'Tá mé tuirseach,' arsa Máire.   ('I am tired,' said Máire.)
  'Cá bhfuil tú?' arsa mise.       ('Where are you?' said I.)
  'Tar isteach,' arsa sé.           ('Come in,' said he.)
  arsa never takes person endings — it is invariable. It is followed by a pronoun or name.

THE FIXED FORM 'DAR':
  dar liom / dar leat / dar leis, etc. — in my/your/his opinion; it seems to me:
  Dar liom, tá sé fíor.  (In my opinion / it seems to me it is true.)
  Dar Dia! / Dar mo choinsias! — By God! / By my conscience! (exclamations)
  dar is defective — it only appears in these set phrases.

SUPPLETIVE VERBAL NOUNS (irregular VN forms of common verbs):
  téigh (go) — verbal noun: ag dul  (NOT *ag téamh)
  tar  (come) — verbal noun: ag teacht (NOT *ag tara)
  abair (say) — verbal noun: ag rá    (NOT *ag abairt)
  feic (see) — verbal noun: ag feiceáil / ag féachaint
  These must be learned as irregular forms.

examples.irish: Is cuimhin liom an lá sin go maith.
Dar liom, ní raibh sé ann in aon chor.
examples.english: In my opinion, he wasn't there at all.
She didn't care about the weather. (past of is cuma le)

examples.irish: Is oth liom é sin a rá.
examples.english: I am sorry to say that.

examples.irish: Is léir dom nach n-oibríonn sé.
examples.english: It is clear to me that it doesn't work.

examples.irish: Tá siad ag dul abhaile. (NOT *ag téamh)
examples.english: They are going home. (suppletive VN of téigh)

notes: The copula-based mental state constructions (is cuimhin, is eol, etc.) are semantically like verbs but grammatically copula sentences. They do not have a progressive form — you cannot say *tá mé ag cuimhneamh in the sense of 'I remember' (though tá mé ag cuimhneamh air means 'I am thinking about it/remembering it' — different nuance). The quotative arsa should not be confused with abair (to say) in its other forms.
